articles.title: Severe Storms Trigger Hundreds of Flight Cancellations and Travel Disruptions This Thanksgiving
articles.summary: More than 350 flights were cancelled and 700 delayed as storms hit the US coasts during Thanksgiving travel, prompting runway closures and emergency declarations, BBC News reports.
articles.content:
More than 350 flights across the United States have been cancelled on Thursday, with an additional 700 flights delayed, as a series of storms sweep the country during the peak of Thanksgiving travel. The disruptions come as the National Weather Service warned of heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding along both the western and eastern seaboards. The Federal Aviation Administration had already cautioned that the forecast weather could cause delays throughout the week, and the latest figures from flight‑tracking service FlightAware show a sharp rise in cancellations and hold‑ups.

The weather‑related challenges were compounded by an incident at Miami International Airport on Wednesday evening. A FedEx cargo aircraft overshot the runway, prompting the FAA to temporarily ground all departures for the airport while investigators examined the cause. No injuries were reported, and the airline released a statement saying the flight "experienced an issue upon landing" and that the crew was safe. An airport employee, speaking on condition of anonymity, suggested that the heavy rain and wind may have prevented the pilot from stopping in time.

The Miami incident occurred just eleven weeks after a separate cargo plane crash at the same airport that resulted in five fatalities on the ground and five injuries. Following the overrun, all but one runway at Miami International were closed for a short period, extending delays for passengers and cargo operators already strained by the holiday travel surge.

Across the nation, the Thanksgiving travel period was expected to involve more than 80 million Americans, according to projections from the American Automobile Association. The AAA also identified Miami as one of the top five domestic destinations for holiday travelers, underscoring the impact of the airport shutdown on a heavily trafficked hub.

On the East Coast, the National Weather Service forecast a powerful storm system to hit Thursday, bringing high winds, heavy rainfall and the risk of major coastal flooding. In anticipation of the threat, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency, citing the potential for renewed flooding in areas that had already experienced inundation earlier in the autumn. In New York City, organizers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Parade responded to the same forecast by moving the event from Thursday to Saturday.

The West Coast faced a parallel set of challenges as a series of Pacific storms were expected to deliver rain, mountain snow and strong winds. King tides—exceptionally high sea levels that occur when astronomical and meteorological factors align—were projected to peak along the coastline during the holiday period. The National Weather Service warned that water levels along California's extensive shoreline could exceed eight feet in some locations, potentially breaking records set only weeks earlier. Residents and officials in coastal communities prepared for the possibility of flooding as the tides coincided with the incoming storms.

Storms were also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, extending the threat into the Canadian province of British Columbia. The combination of rain, wind and elevated tides raised concerns about infrastructure resilience and the safety of travelers in the region.

The FAA's earlier warning about nationwide delays proved prescient. On Wednesday, FlightAware logged more than 6,800 delayed flights and over 160 cancellations, a figure that rose sharply as the weather system intensified on Thursday. The agency's brief grounding of flights bound for Miami highlighted the delicate balance between maintaining safety and preserving the flow of holiday traffic.

Background information: The Federal Aviation Administration oversees the safety and efficiency of civil aviation in the United States, issuing directives such as temporary groundings when safety concerns arise. King tides are the highest predicted water levels of the year, caused by the alignment of the moon and sun with the Earth's orbital position, and can exacerbate coastal flooding when combined with storm surge.

As the Thanksgiving week progresses, travelers continue to navigate a landscape of delayed flights, airport closures and weather alerts. Airlines and airports are working to restore normal operations while authorities monitor the evolving storm systems. The situation illustrates how seasonal travel peaks can be amplified by severe weather, creating widespread logistical challenges for both passengers and the aviation industry.

articles.title: US Firm Gordon Brothers Accused Over Poundland Collapse
articles.summary: Gordon Brothers, who bought Poundland for £1, face criticism for debt demands and cash restrictions that may have hindered a sale, while administrators weigh options amid industry doubts.
articles.content:
The discount retailer Poundland has entered administration after a protracted period of financial strain, prompting a dispute over responsibility between its US owner Gordon Brothers and the company’s management team. The chain, once a staple of low‑price shopping, now faces the prospect of being sold in parts or closed entirely.

Gordon Brothers acquired Poundland for a nominal sum of £1 and subsequently extended an £85 million loan intended to keep the business operating for the 17 months following the purchase. During that time the firm withdrew roughly £20 million, which it says largely covered interest on the loan. The owners are now owed a further £22.5 million, a sum that will rank among the first liabilities to be settled from any future sale proceeds.

Poundland’s internal team argues that the owners’ control over the company’s cash flow prevented the chain from restocking adequately ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period. They point to a modest sales uptick in October as evidence that the business still had growth potential if given sufficient working capital.

Members of the parliamentary Business Committee have publicly criticised Gordon Brothers, using terms such as "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping" to describe the firm’s actions. Their comments reflect broader political concern about the impact of distressed‑asset specialists on retail employment.

Potential purchasers have so far been reluctant to meet the debt terms imposed by Gordon Brothers. Martin Property Group proposed an upfront payment of £5 million with the remainder deferred, while Xyra Holdings offered £12.5 million up front but were reportedly unable to fulfil the commitment. Both offers were hampered by the requirement to settle the outstanding loan.

Gordon Brothers contests the portrayal of its role, insisting that the loan was necessary to prevent an earlier collapse that they claim would have occurred in June of the previous year. The firm maintains that the £20 million extracted from the business primarily represented interest accrued on the financing they provided.

Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with the previous year, Poundland failed to generate sufficient cash flow to sustain operations. Forecasts indicated that sales would fall short of expectations by about £115 million, a shortfall that eclipsed the impact of a £100 million cost‑cutting programme the company had implemented.

The retailer also suffered from sector‑wide pressures, including rising labour costs, higher employment taxes and increased business rates, all of which have strained margins across the discount‑store market.

Gordon Brothers argues that none of the interested parties could satisfy the financial and operational criteria required to take over the chain, citing a lack of both capital and expertise to revive the business. The firm suggests that its continued support allowed the company to remain open for an additional 17 months, thereby preserving thousands of jobs.

The chair of the Business Committee has called for another meeting with Gordon Brothers and Poundland’s management to clarify the disputed facts and assess whether alternative arrangements could have been pursued.

Industry observers note that a new bidder could still emerge, though many consider this unlikely. Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told BBC News: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome." She added that a breakup of the chain now appears more probable.

In the UK, administrators are appointed to oversee insolvent companies, with the aim of maximising returns for creditors by either selling the business as a whole or liquidating its assets. Their decisions are guided by legal obligations to treat all secured and unsecured creditors fairly.

If the chain is broken up, many of the stores are expected to find new owners who will rely on local staff familiar with the market. However, workers face significant uncertainty just weeks before the holiday season, a period that traditionally brings the highest footfall and revenue for discount retailers.

Gordon Brothers specialises in managing companies in commercial distress, seeking to ensure that even the worst outcomes generate a return on their investment. In this case, the firm stands to recover its £22.5 million claim, earn interest on the loan secured against Poundland’s assets, and collect additional fees, a structure that critics argue reduces the incentive to secure a swift sale.

The contrasting narratives highlight the complexity of distressed‑asset transactions, where the interests of creditors, employees and potential buyers can diverge sharply, leaving the future of iconic high‑street brands like Poundland uncertain.

articles.title: Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Parade Delayed to Saturday Amid East Coast Storm
articles.summary: Organisers postponed the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday because of a severe East Coast storm, citing safety concerns for participants and spectators.
articles.content:
Organisers of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade announced Wednesday that the event, traditionally held on Thanksgiving, will be moved to Saturday after Black Friday because an approaching East Coast storm threatens turbulent weather. The decision shifts the centennial parade, a milestone for the New York‑based retailer, to a later date to protect participants and viewers. According to reporting by Al Jazeera, this marks the first postponement in the parade’s history.

The parade, a long‑standing Thanksgiving tradition, features massive helium‑filled balloons, elaborate floats, marching bands and celebrity performers that travel along a Manhattan route. It is broadcast nationwide and draws millions of on‑site spectators, making it a central part of the holiday celebration for many Americans. The spectacle showcases a mix of popular culture icons and seasonal themes, with the route running down major avenues that allow crowds to line the streets and watch the towering balloons ascend.

National Weather Service alerts warned of gusts approaching ninety‑seven kilometres per hour and rain accumulations of up to five centimetres for Thursday and Friday, with a high‑wind warning in effect from early Thursday through early Friday. Officials also warned of possible coastal flooding that could affect low‑lying parts of the city. City officials cited the forecast as the primary reason for postponing the procession, noting the potential for lashing winds and flooding that could endanger both the inflated balloons and the crowd along the route.

Will Coss, Macy’s executive producer, told reporters, "While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our participants and spectators is and always will be our top priority." He added that the organization remains hopeful about delivering the most spectacular centennial parade.

The centennial parade was already in the final stages of preparation when the delay was announced, with signature balloons being inflated on Wednesday. New additions include a five‑storey‑tall balloon of the cartoon character Bluey wearing a crown, a seventeen‑metre‑long Snoopy balloon carrying Woodstock, and a blue hippopotamus that pays homage to a historic balloon that drifted away in an early parade, highlighting the event’s long history.

Macy’s website listed a lineup of musical and theatrical talent slated for the event, featuring singers such as Raye and Wyclef Jean, as well as Broadway performers Leslie Odom Jr and Anthony Ramos. These performers are expected to appear on the floats or on a stage set up along the route, adding musical interludes to the visual display. It remains uncertain whether the full roster will appear on Saturday, but the announced acts underscore the parade’s role as a platform for high‑profile entertainment.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first," and assured residents that Saturday’s sky‑high balloons will be safe for all viewers. He also highlighted an expanded police presence along the parade route for Saturday, stating that the New York Police Department is fully prepared for an event of this scale, as it has been for the ninety‑nine previous parades.

Law enforcement will coordinate with emergency services to manage crowd flow and respond to any incidents, ensuring a smooth progression of the procession. The mayor emphasized that no specific or credible threats have been identified, aiming to reassure the public about security and crowd management.

NBC, which traditionally airs the live parade, indicated it will substitute the scheduled broadcast with a repeat of the 2025 edition on Thursday. The repeat broadcast will feature the full ceremony of the previous year, giving viewers a glimpse of the parade’s scale while the live show is delayed.

City authorities estimate that the procession typically attracts more than three and a half million spectators along its Manhattan path. Despite the shift, the anticipated crowd size remains high, reflecting the parade’s status as a cultural touchstone for both residents and tourists. The postponement disrupts a familiar holiday ritual for many families, but officials expect that the Saturday timing will still allow a large audience to experience the centennial celebration, both in person and through television.

Since its founding in 1924, the parade has been cancelled only during World War II, making this the first instance of a postponement rather than a cancellation. The decision to postpone rather than cancel reflects a balance between preserving the historic continuity and adapting to unforeseen weather challenges.

The rescheduled parade is set to begin at half past eight in the morning on Saturday, according to the organizers. As the storm moves out, city officials and Macy’s aim to deliver a safe and memorable centennial event, fulfilling the tradition that has become synonymous with Thanksgiving.

articles.title: One Third of Young Britons Never Had Sex Amid Rising Porn and Sexting
articles.summary: A new Natsal survey shows a third of 16‑24‑year‑olds have never had sex, while half exchange sexual images and most view pornography, with overall declines in sexual activity across adults.
articles.content:
BBC News reported that the latest round of the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) has revealed a marked shift in sexual behaviour among British teenagers and young adults. The study, which interviewed 6,700 people aged 16 to 59 selected at random across the country, is the first to ask about online sexual activities such as sexting and pornography consumption.

Among respondents aged 16 to 24, one in three said they had never had sexual intercourse, a rise from one in five in the previous survey conducted twelve years earlier. At the same time, half of this age group reported sending or receiving sexual images on their mobile phones within the past year, and the majority reported viewing pornographic material.

The gender split showed that half of young women and 86% of young men admitted to watching pornography. Overall, more than one in three women across all ages said they had watched porn in the past year, while the proportion of men who had never had sex stood at 28% compared with 38% of women.

When the figures are compared with earlier Natsal rounds, the increase in sexual inactivity among young people is evident. The earlier surveys in 1990, 2000 and 2010 recorded roughly one in five young adults without sexual experience, whereas the current data indicate a jump to about one in three.

The study also highlighted a broader decline in sexual frequency among adults under 45, with the average occurrence falling to twice a month from a weekly rate recorded in 1990. Lifetime sexual partners averaged five, and women reported having sex roughly once a month while men reported twice a month.

Researchers noted that individuals who had never had sex were less likely to use pornography or masturbate, suggesting that online solo activity is not simply a substitute for partnered sex, although the data cannot confirm causation.

Soazig Clifton of University College London said, "When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci‑fi." She added that future research may need to examine the impact of AI on sexual behaviour. Co‑researcher Prof Wendy Macdowall of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine warned, "while it may be tempting to blame screen time for less sex, it's likely many other factors are involved, especially for young people."

Sexting refers to the exchange of sexually explicit messages or images via digital devices, while pornography encompasses visual material intended to arouse sexual interest. Both practices have become commonplace with the proliferation of smartphones and high‑speed internet, allowing private consumption without direct interpersonal contact.

Several contextual factors may be influencing the observed trends. Young people are drinking less alcohol than previous generations and many continue to live with their parents, reducing opportunities for private encounters. Rising mental‑health challenges and the social restrictions imposed by the Covid pandemic have also limited socialising. Additionally, broader conversations about consent may empower young individuals to make more deliberate choices about sexual activity.

The survey found that one in seven women reported ongoing upset about past sexual experiences, and a similar proportion of men expressed shame about certain sexual thoughts or desires. Earlier Natsal data had identified regret over early sexual activity as a common sentiment among those losing their virginity.

Among young women, the use of oral contraceptive pills has declined, while the proportion of women aged 16 to 44 who do not want children has doubled from 8% to 17% over the past decade. These shifts have implications for rates of unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.

Dr Laura Oakley of LSHTM emphasized that understanding the drivers behind these changes—whether economic insecurity, climate anxiety, or shifting life priorities—should be a research priority, given their impact on health, care and family‑planning services.

The Natsal findings provide a comprehensive snapshot of evolving sexual behaviours in Britain, highlighting reduced partnered activity alongside increased digital sexual engagement, and underscore the need for continued monitoring to inform public‑health policy.

articles.title: US Jury Convicts Huawei and Subsidiaries on Multiple Fraud and Theft Charges
articles.summary: A New York federal jury found Huawei and three of its subsidiaries guilty on ten counts including trade‑secret theft and bank fraud, while acquitting the firm of a racketeering charge, according to Al Jazeera.
articles.content:
A federal jury in New York delivered a verdict on Tuesday that found Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei and three of its affiliates guilty on ten of eleven criminal counts. The convictions cover conspiracy to steal trade secrets, wire and bank fraud, money‑laundering conspiracies, and violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The company was cleared only of the most serious allegation of a criminal racketeering conspiracy.

Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the U.S. Department of Justice said the judgment reflected a long‑standing pattern of illicit conduct, stating, "For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception." The department’s statement detailed several specific incidents that formed the basis of the charges.

One case involved a Huawei employee who accessed confidential information about Tappy, a robot created by T‑Mobile, despite a signed nondisclosure agreement between the firms. In a separate incident, engineers were accused of reproducing the source code of Cisco routers, an act that would give Huawei an unfair advantage in networking equipment.

The indictment also described an employee who assumed a false identity to obtain a position at CNEX, a U.S. technology company that had previously expressed a preference not to work directly with Huawei. This deception was presented as part of a broader effort to infiltrate U.S. firms and acquire proprietary technology.

Further allegations linked Huawei to prohibited activities in Iran and North Korea, nations subject to U.S. sanctions. Prosecutors said the company concealed these dealings from banks and U.S. officials, violating both sanctions law and financial regulations.

The jury’s findings encompass Huawei Device Co Ltd, its Chinese subsidiary, as well as U.S.-based entities Futurewei Technologies Inc. and Huawei Device USA Inc. All were found guilty of the same set of offenses, underscoring the Department of Justice’s view that the misconduct was coordinated across the corporate structure.

Sentencing is scheduled for September, and Huawei’s legal team has indicated that it will pursue an appeal of the verdict. The company’s lawyers have argued that the prosecution relied on isolated misdeeds by a few employees to portray a broader conspiracy.

Beijing responded swiftly, condemning the decision as an attempt by Washington to suppress Chinese enterprises. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement asserting, "The Chinese government firmly opposes movies by the US side aimed at containing and suppressing Chinese enterprises, and firmly supports Chinese enterprises’ lawful rights."

The verdict arrives amid heightened tensions in the global technology arena, where the United States and China are competing for dominance in artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductor capabilities. Recent scrutiny of the chipmaker Nvidia, whose products power many AI systems, highlights the broader context of U.S. efforts to limit Chinese access to cutting‑edge technology.

Background: Trade secrets refer to confidential business information that provides a competitive edge, such as designs, formulas, or processes. Unauthorized acquisition or disclosure of such information is illegal under U.S. law. The International Emergency Economic Powers Act grants the president authority to regulate economic transactions during national emergencies, and violations can result in criminal penalties. Wire fraud involves using electronic communications to deceive others for financial gain, while bank fraud pertains to schemes that defraud financial institutions.

The case against Huawei reflects a pattern of enforcement actions targeting Chinese technology firms accused of breaching U.S. sanctions and intellectual‑property rules. Over recent years, U.S. authorities have increased scrutiny of foreign entities operating in sensitive sectors, citing concerns over national security and the integrity of the financial system.

According to reporting by Al Jazeera, the convictions mark a significant legal setback for Huawei, which has faced restrictions and bans in several Western markets. The outcome may influence ongoing debates about how to balance open innovation with security safeguards in an increasingly interconnected digital economy.

While the company prepares for sentencing and an appeal, the broader implications for the global telecommunications industry remain uncertain. Competitors and partners will be watching how the enforcement of these statutes shapes future collaborations and supply‑chain decisions.

The United States has also pursued actions against other technology firms, exemplified by the investigation into Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang for alleged leaks of sensitive information to China. Nvidia, a leading supplier of AI‑focused chips, has been subject to export controls that limit sales of its most advanced products to Chinese customers, reflecting a wider policy of curbing technology transfer.

Overall, the jury’s decision underscores the U.S. government’s determination to enforce laws governing trade secrets, sanctions compliance, and financial fraud, particularly when national security considerations are invoked.

articles.title: Trust crisis in NHS Grampian tests Scottish government’s response
articles.summary: Recent watchdog findings and a surgeon’s whistleblowing expose avoidable deaths at NHS Grampian, prompting an independent review and raising political stakes for First Minister John Swinney, BBC News reports.
articles.content:
Trust in the National Health Service in Scotland’s north‑east has been severely tested after a series of revelations about NHS Grampian’s performance. Patients, families and health professionals have been urged to consider whether the system delivers the standards it promises, and whether political leaders are adequately informed.

A report from Healthcare Improvement Scotland highlighted serious flaws in the board’s leadership and clinical governance. The watchdog warned of repeated, avoidable harm and questioned the board’s capacity to learn from serious adverse events. These findings have amplified concerns about the effectiveness of senior management across the NHS.

The issue gained a personal dimension when Dr Mohammed Habib, a surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, disclosed a previously unpublished 2022 review of the hospital’s liver and pancreatic unit. The review examined 45 patients treated over seven years, noting that 31 had died and that 19 of those deaths were judged potentially avoidable. Dr Habib said he had raised these concerns for a decade, but the data were not made public by NHS Grian or the Scottish government.

Dr Habib also said he wrote to the first minister on three occasions, seeking a response. At a Holyrood question‑time session, First Minister John Swinney described the matters as being of the "gravest concern" and said officials had given "appropriate responses" by directing the surgeon to a national whistle‑blowing service and to the police. However, his office later claimed it had not been personally briefed on the correspondence, prompting questions about the flow of information to the highest political office.

In reaction to the mounting pressure, the Scottish government dispatched a support team to assist NHS Grampian’s management, though the suitability of some appointees has been questioned due to problems in their own areas of responsibility. Health Secretary Angela Constance announced an independent review to determine who knew what, when they knew it, and how the information was handled. The review will be led by an experienced King’s Counsel from outside Scotland, with clinical input also sourced externally. Constance emphasized that the findings will be published in full and that any urgent issues identified will be reported directly to the relevant bodies.

Constance also rejected claims that no action followed the 2022 review compiled by University of Edinburgh professor Stephen Wigmore. She explained that liver and pancreatic surgery was temporarily halted, then resumed under the professor’s supervision until he was satisfied that it could continue safely. The service was stopped again on at least two further occasions, and patients requiring complex procedures have been transferred to NHS Lothian since early this year.

Former Health Secretary Humza Yousaf and chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith have been identified as having been aware of the 2022 review. Yousaf has publicly pledged full scrutiny and "further dramatic action" in NHS Grampian, while Sir Gregor has not yet commented publicly.

The situation is likely to generate further parliamentary scrutiny, with the possibility of senior figures being called before a Holyrood committee. Police investigations are also underway to decide whether a formal inquiry is warranted. Some observers have suggested that a judge‑led public inquiry may eventually be needed, although such inquiries can be lengthy and costly. Scotland already hosts three health‑related public inquiries into Covid‑19 handling, major hospital building projects, and a botched brain surgery case.

Background: whistleblowing is a process by which individuals raise concerns about wrongdoing or unsafe practices within an organization, often protected by law to encourage reporting without fear of retaliation. Independent reviews, such as the one ordered by the Scottish government, are external examinations that assess the actions of officials and institutions, aiming to provide transparency and recommendations for improvement.

The political dimension of the episode is significant. Critics argue that the first minister’s office may lack a clear system for filtering and escalating serious health‑service concerns, a gap that could undermine public confidence. Swinney’s rapid request for a civil‑service review of correspondence handling suggests an awareness of the potential damage to his administration’s credibility.

At the same time, the Scottish government is pursuing a broader reform of the NHS structure. Plans are under discussion to consolidate the existing network of regional health boards into two bodies covering mainland Scotland. Proponents claim that a more centralized system could deliver stronger oversight and faster responses to problems, while opponents warn that it might mask local deficiencies and reduce accountability.

The convergence of these issues – a watchdog report, a surgeon’s whistleblowing, political scrutiny, and systemic reform proposals – creates a complex challenge for the Scottish administration. Restoring public trust will require clear communication, demonstrable action on the findings of the independent review, and assurance that mechanisms exist to prevent similar failures in the future.

As the review proceeds, families of affected patients and health‑care professionals are likely to continue sharing their experiences, potentially prompting further investigations. The outcome will shape not only the future of NHS Grampian but also the broader debate over how Scotland’s health service should be organised and overseen.

Ultimately, the government must convince both the public and political opponents that it has a firm grasp of the situation in NHS Grampian, ensuring that patients can once again place their trust in the vital services the NHS provides.

articles.title: Energy bills to jump 26% in January as gas prices surge
articles.summary: BBC News reports a 26% rise in household energy costs from January, driven by higher wholesale gas prices linked to the Iran war, with government payments and discounts offered amid growing debt concerns.
articles.content:
BBC News reported that the energy price cap will lift by 26% for millions of households starting in January, marking the steepest increase since the price shock caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The rise reflects a sharp climb in wholesale gas costs, which regulators say have risen by a third over the three months used to set the new cap and have more than doubled since late 2025.

For a household that pays by direct debit and consumes a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland or Wales, the annual bill is projected to move from £1,723 to £2,166 if the higher rates persist for a full year. In practical terms, the average monthly bill could be about £37 higher in the first quarter of the year, with winter months potentially seeing an extra £60 per month depending on usage.

To soften the impact, the government will provide a £100 payment to up to 20 million households in England from 4 January, with comparable schemes in Scotland and Wales. In addition, the warm‑home discount will shave £150 off the bills of six million benefit claimants this winter. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh warned that families will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills, adding, "For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets."

The energy price cap is a regulatory tool that limits the maximum unit price that suppliers can charge on default tariffs. It is reviewed every three months based on the wholesale costs suppliers face and the expenses of running the national energy system. The cap sets a ceiling for each kilowatt‑hour rather than the total bill, meaning that customers on fixed‑term contracts are insulated until their agreements end, while those on variable deals see immediate changes.

The surge in wholesale gas prices is attributed primarily to the Iran war, according to Ofgem. Suppliers have passed the higher wholesale costs onto consumers, resulting in unit price increases from 7.97p to 10.96p for gas and from 26.32p to 32.69p for electricity per kilowatt‑hour. Daily standing charges will rise to 29.65p for gas and 54.77p for electricity.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice. Ofgem’s director general for markets, Neil Kenward, said the regulator has reminded suppliers of their duties to identify vulnerable customers early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable.

Charities and campaign groups such as Friends of the Earth and Global Witness have criticised major oil and energy firms for recording large profits amid soaring oil costs, arguing that households bear the brunt. Energy UK, representing the suppliers, countered that profit caps on a percentage basis limit the gains for bill‑issuing companies, although higher overall bills still translate into larger nominal cash profits.

Customers on prepayment meters are expected to feel the pressure most acutely, as they must pay for energy at the point of use rather than spreading costs over the year. Those on variable tariffs will see the new unit rates immediately, while fixed‑term customers remain on their existing rates until contract expiry.

Labour’s shadow energy secretary, Andrew Bowie, described the situation as an outrage, accusing the government of adding green levies and taxes to already soaring bills and signing the country up to an EU scheme that could push costs higher.

Stacey, a 40‑year‑old single mother from Bristol, described her coping strategy as a "battle" and said she has lowered her central heating from 22°C to 19.5°C, uses electric blankets, keeps curtains closed and dresses her children in thermal clothing. She pays her bills by direct debit and limits washing machine use to Sundays.

Industry observers anticipate a rise in household debt and a surge in requests for emergency assistance. Citizens Advice warned that the £100 payment may be quickly exhausted, especially for prepayment‑meter users, leading to a wave of emergency support claims. Energy UK criticised the targeting of the payment as inadequate, while the government indicated that local councils have a £100 million discretionary fund to aid vulnerable households outside the main scheme.

Overall, the combination of higher wholesale costs, the new cap levels and limited support measures creates a challenging winter for consumers, with the regulator and government urging early identification of those at risk and urging suppliers to keep repayment arrangements manageable.

articles.title: US Voters Majority Favor Immediate End to Iran War, Poll Shows
articles.summary: A Critical Issues Poll finds 55% of Americans want the US‑Israel conflict with Iran stopped now, with strong backing from Democrats and independents, and growing pressure on Congress to cut funding.
articles.content:
A new Critical Issues Poll released by the University of Maryland and Ipsos indicates that a clear majority of American voters want the United States to end its involvement in the US‑Israel war on Iran without waiting for any particular settlement. The reporting comes from Al Jazeera, which relayed the findings of the survey of 1,022 adults across the country.

Overall, 55 percent of respondents said they support an immediate end to the war regardless of the terms that might be reached. Support was especially high among Democrats, with 80 percent in favor, and among independents, where 59 percent agreed. About a quarter of Republican respondents expressed the same preference.

Among Democratic voters, there was also notable backing for measures that would pressure the Trump administration to halt the conflict. Fifty‑three percent said they would favor Congress withholding funding for military operations, while 51 percent indicated they would back an “Iran war‑funding cutoff” in upcoming budget negotiations, even if such a move risked a government shutdown.

The poll asked participants to choose among three possible courses of action: ending the conflict immediately, escalating militarily, or continuing the current strategy in order to extract concessions from Iran. Only 21 percent favored maintaining the current path, and 18 percent supported escalation, leaving a clear preference for an immediate cease‑fire.

"Clearly, the public mood is to end it now, whatever it takes," said Shibley Telhami, the poll’s principal investigator, during a phone interview. He added that the level of support for ending the war surprised him, noting that while many people opposed the conflict, the extent of what they would accept to achieve peace was less certain.

Voters also appear skeptical of the government’s justification for the war. Only 28 percent believed that the conflict had placed Iran in a worse position to develop nuclear weapons. The United States has long expressed concern that Iran could pursue a nuclear arsenal, although intelligence assessments have not found evidence of an authorized nuclear weapons program since Tehran abandoned such ambitions in 2003.

Background: The United States has maintained a policy of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons capability, viewing a nuclear‑armed Iran as a threat to regional stability and to U.S. interests. Congressional funding decisions can influence the scope and duration of military engagements, and a funding cutoff would require the executive branch to adjust its operations accordingly.

The war has also affected the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil supply passes. Early in the conflict, Iran closed the strait to commercial traffic, prompting the Trump administration to impose a naval blockade. The poll found that 35 percent of respondents believed Iran now controls the strait, while just 12.7 percent thought the United States holds that control. The disruption contributed to higher fuel prices.

Politically, the Democratic Party is debating how far to go in ending the unpopular war. The recent midterm elections saw a backlash against the conflict and related issues such as rising fuel costs, contributing to significant gains for Democrats and a loss of congressional control for Republicans. Within the Democratic caucus, anti‑war members of the party’s left have pointed to the poll results as evidence that voters demand an end to the war and to U.S. support for Israel.

However, this stance has created tension with the party’s more hawkish establishment wing. Leaders such as Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer have expressed support for ending the war but have not yet committed to aggressive measures such as cutting off military funding or leveraging upcoming budget battles to force a cease‑fire.

"A lot of Democratic figures are dismissing the intensity of public feeling on this issue," Telhami warned, adding that failure to adapt could leave those leaders behind. Progressive senators, including Bernie Sanders and Chris Van Hollen, have been among those urging a more assertive approach. Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer for Senate leadership, has used the war to portray moderate party leadership as out of step with voters.

The poll indicated that Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer by a ratio of nearly three to one, underscoring the political pressure on Senate leaders to respond to public sentiment.

The findings suggest that public opinion could shape upcoming congressional debates over funding for the conflict and may influence the strategies that both parties adopt as they navigate the war’s domestic political ramifications.

articles.title: Guardians sign Kris Bubic as Cubs eye Japanese pitcher Kaima Taira
articles.summary: The Cleveland Guardians have added left‑hander Kris Bubic on a one‑year deal, while the Chicago Cubs are reportedly targeting Japanese right‑hander Kaima Taira amid a busy offseason shaped by looming lockout talks.
articles.content:
The 2026‑27 Major League Baseball offseason is already being defined by uncertainty. Ongoing collective bargaining negotiations and the near‑certain prospect of an owner‑initiated lockout on Dec. 2 are prompting clubs to accelerate trades and free‑agent signings, a pattern that echoed the 2021‑22 lockout period. Recent high‑profile moves illustrate that trend: the New York Mets secured ace Tarik Skubal on a record contract, the Chicago Cubs bolstered their rotation with Trevor Rogers and added outfielder Teruaki Sato, and Freddy Peralta was dealt to the Baltimore Orioles. Analysts expect additional activity before a lockout could take effect.

Daily rumor round‑ups are tracking the flow of information, and today’s focus includes two notable targets. The Chicago Cubs, still rebuilding after losing several contributors to free agency, are reportedly interested in right‑hander Kaima Taira, a 27‑year‑old pitcher who was posted from Japan on Nov. 1. Taira, who spent 2024 and 2025 as a reliever for the Seibu Lions before starting in 2026, is praised for his low release point that creates a deceptive delivery. The Athletic’s scouting note reads: "Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it." He throws a mid‑90s four‑seam fastball backed by a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup and splitter, though his breaking balls are described as merely adequate. Because pitchers of his stature often struggle with a starter’s workload, the Cubs may initially use him in a multi‑inning relief role before considering a full‑time start.

International free agents like Taira must navigate the posting system, which allows Japanese teams to make a player available to MLB clubs for a set fee. Once posted, the player can negotiate with any interested MLB organization, and the original team receives a posting fee based on the contract’s value. This mechanism has produced several successful transitions, though outcomes vary depending on how clubs integrate the talent.

In Cleveland, the Guardians have reached a free‑agent agreement with left‑hander Kris Bubic. ESPN reports the deal is worth $17.5 million for a single season. Bubic, 29, logged nine starts for the Kansas City Royals last year before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers, where he shifted to a bullpen role. His fastball is noted for an unusual rise and release point, giving him a high ceiling as a starter, though a history of injuries could see him deployed out of the bullpen. The Athletic described him as an "interesting \"ceiling\" candidate in the rotation."

One‑year contracts like Bubic’s are common for teams seeking immediate depth while preserving flexibility. A pitcher with a strong fastball but injury concerns often receives a short‑term deal that allows a club to evaluate durability without a long‑term commitment. If the player remains healthy, he may earn a longer contract; otherwise, the team can reassess after the season.

The Minnesota Twins, having re‑signed veteran starter Sonny Gray, continue to search for roster upgrades aimed at a 2027 contention push. According to the Athletic, the Twins’ priority list includes a first baseman or second baseman and an additional left‑handed reliever, indicating a focus on both offensive balance and bullpen depth.

Even after landing Skubal, the Mets appear ready to explore further pitching options. The Athletic notes that New York may pursue a short‑term starter for the 2027 season, a strategy that would limit the team to the later stages of the market as many marquee free agents secure contracts earlier in the offseason.

All of these moves are unfolding against the backdrop of a potential lockout, a scenario that could compress the timeline for transactions and force clubs to finalize deals quickly. As the deadline approaches, MLB teams are likely to continue weighing risk and reward, balancing immediate needs with long‑term plans. CBS Sports reported the latest developments, and the offseason is expected to remain active until the lockout deadline arrives.

articles.title: Young workers hide dyslexia amid workplace challenges
articles.summary: A BBC News report highlights how many dyslexic employees conceal their condition, the stress it causes, and calls for better workplace support.
articles.content:
Ayana Bailey, a nineteen-year-old part‑time florist, often chooses not to disclose her dyslexia on job applications because she worries it could affect her chances. She explains that while she does not expect overt discrimination, the uncertainty makes her hesitant to reveal the condition.

A survey conducted by the British Dyslexia Association with more than one thousand two hundred working adults who are dyslexic shows that nearly half keep their diagnosis hidden at work. Over four‑fifths of respondents say the condition adds to their work‑related stress, and more than half report feeling bad about themselves because of it.

Bailey was diagnosed at the age of eleven and received supportive mentoring at school, which helped her recognise her strengths and cope with low self‑esteem. Transitioning to employment, however, has proved more demanding. She describes the application process as daunting and relies on her mother to review forms with her. In interviews she says she "just shut down. I completely forget who I am," and she sometimes prepares a brief script to manage the situation, though it does not always succeed.

Despite the anxiety, Bailey believes dyslexia contributes positively to her creativity and ability to think outside conventional frameworks. She identifies visual learning as a key strength, allowing her to picture characters before reading descriptions, an asset for her ambition to work in the creative arts and eventually become a casting director.

Nurse Lisa Daniels, aged thirty‑seven, recounts how her dyslexia once forced her to stay at work well beyond her shift to complete paperwork. She admits she initially suppressed the impact, telling herself everything was fine, but later recognised the significant effect on her performance. A former manager dismissed her request for adjustments, labeling the need for accommodations as "babying" staff. Daniels eventually learned about a neurodiversity staff network, which boosted her confidence and led to practical changes such as noise‑cancelling headphones. She now describes herself as resilient, continuing to show up despite limited support, and says she has moved beyond imposter syndrome.

The BDA’s findings indicate that many dyslexic employees must expend extra effort to compensate for inaccessible systems, processes and communication. The association estimates that three point three million dyslexic adults are currently employed and urges employers to implement reasonable adjustments even for staff without a formal diagnosis. It also calls for manager training to better understand and support dyslexic workers.

Personal testimonies collected for the report illustrate everyday challenges: comments framed as banter about spelling, the need to constantly prove intellectual capability, and experiences where early disclosure was used against the employee. Some respondents note that having a line manager who is also dyslexic creates a supportive environment where they can exchange best practices.

Legal precedent underscores the importance of accommodation. Employment law solicitor Jenna Ide helped a client secure a high‑profile discrimination ruling against a major coffee chain in 2016. Ide observes that many dyslexic employees begin new roles already battling low self‑esteem, especially those diagnosed later in life after years of believing they were not intelligent enough. When employers rely on inaccessible practices and fail to offer support, it reinforces negative self‑perceptions and discourages requests for help.

Kate Griggs, founder of the charity Made By Dyslexia, stresses that recruitment processes heavily weighted toward written applications and timed tests can act as barriers. She advises young dyslexic individuals to recognise and own their strengths, communicate them confidently, request necessary support, and seek roles that value their particular abilities.

Background: Dyslexia is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects the way the brain processes written language. It often manifests as difficulties with reading, spelling and decoding, while individuals may excel in visual‑spatial reasoning, problem‑solving and creative thinking. Workplace accommodations can include alternative communication formats, adjustable fonts, colour contrasts and assistive technologies, which help level the playing field for those with dyslexia.

Ellen Broomé, head of the British Dyslexia Association, emphasizes that the extra time and energy spent compensating for unsupportive environments represents a hidden cost. She asserts that the issue is not about ability or ambition, but about removing barriers that prevent talented individuals from contributing fully.

The report’s broader message calls for a cultural shift in employment practices, urging organizations to recognise diverse cognitive styles and to implement inclusive policies that allow dyslexic employees to thrive without having to work harder for the same opportunities. This aligns with the growing awareness that neurodiversity can enrich workplaces when properly supported.

articles.title: Appeals Court Revives Trump’s Attempt to Move Hush‑Money Case to Federal Court
articles.summary: A 2nd Circuit panel reversed a district judge’s denial, allowing a federal judge to consider moving former President Donald Trump’s New York hush‑money conviction to federal court, according to Al Jazeera.
articles.content:
A three‑judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit issued a two‑page order on Monday that overturns a lower‑court decision and restores former President Donald Trump’s request to shift his New York criminal case to federal jurisdiction. The panel found that the district judge’s refusal to allow removal was erroneous, and it instructed a Manhattan federal judge to evaluate whether the matter can proceed under federal law.

The appellate panel specifically rejected the reasoning of the late U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who had held that removal was categorically unavailable after a state criminal conviction. By stating that Hellerstein “erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case,” the Second Circuit opened the door for a federal review of the conviction, though the guilty verdict itself remains untouched.

In a statement to the Associated Press, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said the president “appreciates the 2nd Circuit’s prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System.” The comment underscores the administration’s view that the decision corrects a series of procedural setbacks.

The underlying case stems from a payment of $130,000 made shortly before the 2016 election to adult‑film actress Stormy Daniels. Prosecutors allege that the payment, funneled through Trump’s former lawyer Michael Cohen, was intended to silence Daniels about an alleged affair, thereby influencing the election. The indictment asserted that Trump falsified business records to disguise the reimbursement to Cohen as a legitimate legal expense, a maneuver they say violated state election statutes.

In May 2024, a New York jury convicted Trump on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records, marking the first criminal conviction of a sitting U.S. president. At a sentencing hearing in January 2025, he received an unconditional discharge, meaning he faced no prison time or fine, but the conviction remains on his record. Since then, Trump has pursued multiple avenues to overturn the judgment, including the current bid to have the case heard in federal court.

Trump’s legal strategy hinges on the doctrine of presidential immunity, which the Supreme Court affirmed in a 2024 ruling that presidents may enjoy presumptive immunity for official acts performed while in office. His team is expected to argue that the evidence used by New York prosecutors would have been protected by that immunity, and therefore the state conviction should be vacated. The precise scope of “official act” remains unsettled, as the Court has previously limited immunity to actions within the president’s constitutional authority.

Background: Presidential immunity is a legal principle that shields a sitting president from certain lawsuits and prosecutions for actions taken as part of official duties. The doctrine is intended to allow the executive to perform functions without the threat of constant litigation, but courts have drawn lines between official conduct and personal or criminal behavior.

Background: Removal jurisdiction allows a defendant to transfer a case from state to federal court when federal questions are implicated or when diversity of citizenship exists. The process typically requires a petition to a federal judge, who decides whether the statutory criteria for removal are met. If granted, the case proceeds under federal procedural rules.

The appellate decision also pauses Trump’s ongoing appeal in New York’s Appellate Division, which had heard arguments earlier this month but had not yet issued a ruling. By directing a federal judge to consider removal, the Second Circuit effectively stalls the state‑level review until the federal question is resolved.

Judge Hellerstein, who had denied the removal request for the third time, passed away last month at the age of 92, ending a long tenure on the bench. His death adds a procedural footnote to the case but does not affect the appellate court’s order.

The federal judge in Manhattan now faces a directive to rule on the removal request promptly, though no specific deadline has been set. The upcoming decision will determine whether the conviction can be examined under federal jurisdiction, potentially allowing Trump to raise his immunity arguments before a federal tribunal.

articles.title: Trump to hold third private dinner for top $TRUMP coin investors
articles.summary: President Donald Trump will host a private gala for the largest holders of his $TRUMP meme coin, drawing criticism from Democrats over possible conflicts of interest, while the cryptocurrency’s value has fallen sharply.
articles.content:
President Donald Trump is set to host a third exclusive dinner for the biggest investors in his $TRUMP meme coin. The event is scheduled for Sunday at the Trump National Golf Club located just outside Washington, DC, and is being billed as a unique gathering for the cryptocurrency’s elite supporters.

According to the event’s official website, the invitation list comprises the 185 largest $TRUMP holders. Among the confirmed attendees are businessman Kevin O’Leary and former boxing champion Floyd Mayweather. The 29 highest‑ranking holders will gain access to a separate VIP reception where Trump is expected to appear. The site assures participants that "There will be no private meetings with The President. No gifts will be accepted," emphasizing the private nature of the gathering.

Organizers describe the dinner as a once‑in‑a‑lifetime experience that attendees will remember forever. However, Democratic leaders have voiced concerns that the gathering could be used to turn the presidency into a revenue‑generating platform. "Trump is continuing to exploit the presidency for his personal gain," said Kendall Witmer, deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee, in a statement released after the announcement.

The criticism follows an open letter from eight Democratic senators issued in October, which warned of potential conflicts of interest and called for a thorough inquiry into the president’s financial dealings related to the event. The letter argued that the monetization of Trump’s name and likeness raises serious ethical questions and urged a robust investigation.

The political backdrop has shifted since the senators’ letter, with Democrats securing majorities in both chambers of Congress after the November 3 midterm elections. This new balance of power could enable congressional committees to issue subpoenas or launch formal investigations once the incoming members are sworn in next year.

The White House has dismissed the allegations, characterising the dinner as a private affair rather than a government function. Officials have stressed that there is no promise of official action in exchange for attendance and have reiterated that many of Trump’s assets are placed in a trust managed by family members while he holds office.

Trump’s involvement in the cryptocurrency sector extends beyond the meme coin itself. He holds stakes in firms such as World Liberty Financial and has made the promotion of digital assets a hallmark of his second term. Under his administration, the U.S. Treasury created a reserve of digital currency assets, reflecting his ambition to position the United States as a leading hub for crypto activity.

Meme coins are digital tokens that derive their popularity from internet culture and celebrity endorsements. They often experience rapid price swings based on social media hype rather than underlying fundamentals. Trump launched his $TRUMP coin on January 17, 2025, just days before the start of his second presidential term, using the novelty of the token to attract attention and investment.

The current dinner follows two earlier private events aimed at top $TRUMP holders. The first took place on May 22, 2025, at the same golf club, and required participants to own at least $55,000 worth of $TRUMP coins. The second was held on April 25, 2026, at Mar‑a‑Lago, Trump’s Florida resort. During the 2025 gathering, Chinese crypto investor Justin Sun was declared the winner of a contest for holding the most $TRUMP coins, with an estimated portfolio of roughly $18 million in the token and additional holdings in World Liberty Financial. Earlier this year, Sun filed a lawsuit against World Liberty Financial, alleging that the firm froze his assets and prevented him from selling them.

The value of the $TRUMP coin has seen dramatic fluctuations. The token surged to $74 following Trump’s inauguration in January 2025, but its price has since eroded, trading at about $0.88 on the eve of the upcoming gala.

Financial disclosure forms released earlier this year show that Trump earned more than $2.2 billion in 2025, his first year of the second term. A substantial portion of that income, approximately $636 million, came from sales of the $TRUMP meme coin and related digital assets.

The upcoming dinner proceeds amid heightened scrutiny from lawmakers and the public. While the administration maintains that the event is a private gathering with no official government business, the convergence of political power, personal wealth, and a volatile cryptocurrency continues to raise questions about the boundaries between public office and private profit. Al Jazeera reported on the development, noting the ongoing debate over potential conflicts of interest.

articles.title: DK Metcalf Ejected After Eye Poke, Faces Possible Suspension
articles.summary: Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf was tossed from a game against the Eagles after a second unsportsmanlike penalty involving a poke to defender Cooper DeJean, putting him at risk of further discipline.
articles.content:
CBS Sports reported that the Steelers’ veteran receiver DK Metcalb was removed from the contest with Philadelphia after an incident in the third quarter in which he appeared to jab Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean in the eye. The action triggered his second unsportsmanlike conduct penalty of the night and resulted in an automatic ejection under league rules.

The ejection marks the third time Metcalb has been thrown out of an NFL game since entering the league in 2019. His first dismissal occurred in the tenth week of the 2021 season during a loss to the Green Bay Packers, when he grabbed the facemask of safety Henry Black. That episode led to a fine of $6,949. The second ejection came in week fourteen of the 2023 campaign, when he fought San Francisco 49ers linebacker Fred Warner, body‑slamming the player and then seizing his facemask; the league fined him $19,123 for that altercation.

Metcalb’s disciplinary history also includes a $11,941 fine for taunting after Pittsburgh’s week‑four loss to the Cleveland Browns and a two‑game suspension at the end of the 2025 season following a physical confrontation with a Lions fan. The league office is expected to review the latest incident with DeJean to determine whether an additional fine or suspension will be imposed.

During the game in question, the Steelers’ offense struggled to move the ball, and Metcalb recorded only one catch on four targets for two yards. The lone reception came on the opening series, after which the Eagles’ secondary continued to press him, forcing an incomplete pass moments before the confrontation.

Metcalb, a former Pro Bowler with Seattle, is currently in the second year of a four‑year contract valued at $132 million that he signed after Pittsburgh acquired him in a trade. In the 2025 season he posted 59 receptions for 850 yards and six touchdowns, the lowest totals of his career in both categories. Entering the 2026 season he had logged 35 catches for 432 yards and two touchdowns, with a 12.3‑yard average per reception, a 6.2‑yard average per target and a 40.0 percent catch rate, all of which would be career lows if the season concluded at that point.

The Steelers’ receiving group has been described as subpar, and the franchise may consider moving Metcalb during the upcoming offseason. However, his sizable contract is likely to complicate any potential trade negotiations.

"They say it's going to a good cause, so I might as well win Walter Payton Man of the Year," Metcalb said this summer when asked about the frequency of his fines. The comment reflects his awareness of the financial penalties he has incurred throughout his career.

Background: In the NFL, unsportsmanlike conduct penalties are assessed for actions that are deemed overly aggressive, abusive, or detrimental to the spirit of the game. A second unsportsmanlike penalty in a single contest typically results in an automatic ejection, and repeat offenders may face additional discipline such as fines or suspensions. The league’s disciplinary process involves a review by the NFL office, which can impose further sanctions based on the severity and context of the incident.

The incident with DeJean adds to a pattern of on‑field confrontations that have shadowed Metcalb’s tenure in Pittsburgh. While his physical talent remains evident, the accumulation of penalties and disciplinary measures has raised questions about his impact on team cohesion and the potential financial ramifications for the organization.

Pittsburgh will need to address the immediate gap left by Metcalb’s removal from the game and consider how his conduct may affect roster decisions moving forward. The outcome of the league’s review will determine whether additional punitive measures are applied, which could influence both his availability for the remainder of the season and his standing with the Steelers.

The Steelers continue to seek ways to generate offensive production despite challenges at the receiver position, and the situation underscores the broader issue of player discipline within the league.

articles.title: Young Scots Driving Surge in Disability Benefit Claims
articles.summary: Claims for disability benefits in Scotland have risen sharply, especially among younger people and for mental health conditions, raising concerns about the sustainability of the devolved welfare system.
articles.content:
Every month more than 12,000 people apply to Social Security Scotland for disability support, and the total number of claimants has climbed dramatically since the Covid pandemic. Current estimates suggest that the pool of recipients could reach one million by the end of the decade, a level far higher than a few years ago.

The rise mirrors a broader increase in self‑reported disability across the United Kingdom, but the growth is most pronounced in Scotland. The proportion of working‑age adults who say they have a disability rose from 19 % in 2020‑21 to 28 % in 2023‑24, while among children under 16 the share doubled from 6 % to 12 %. Those figures have translated into roughly 800,000 Scots receiving some form of disability payment today.

A shift in the age profile of applicants is a key factor. Since the introduction of the Adult Disability Payment (ADP) in 2022, about 35 % of new claimants have been under 35 and more than half are under 45. Mental health conditions dominate the ADP caseload, accounting for 41 % of claims, with almost half of those classified as neurotic or stress‑related disorders such as anxiety and post‑traumatic stress disorder. By contrast, before social security was devolved, mental and behavioural disorders made up only 26 % of Personal Independence Payment claims across the UK.

Among children, mental health issues now represent 64 % of applications for the Child Disability Payment. The number of youngsters receiving that benefit has more than doubled, rising from 30,000 in 2020 to 75,000 this year. For older claimants receiving the Pension Age Disability Payment, mental health conditions form a much smaller share, about 13 %, with musculoskeletal and circulatory problems being more common.

Some commentators dismiss the trend as a symptom of an overly sensitive younger generation, but mental‑health charities highlight deeper concerns. Billy Watson, chief executive of Scottish Action for Mental Health, said young people are "growing up significantly more mentally distressed" and face a relentless pace of life amplified by social media and constant exposure to unsettling news.

Disability benefits are payments provided by the state to individuals whose health conditions limit their ability to work or carry out daily activities. They are intended to offset additional costs associated with living with a disability and to provide a safety net for those whose earnings are affected by long‑term health problems.

An independent review for the UK government warned that the surge in mental‑health‑related claims may reflect not only genuine need but also diagnostic practices. Prof Peter Fonagy warned that "diagnosis has become the primary gateway to support that could and should be available earlier", and cautioned that this could increase the risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis. Alan Milburn, author of a UK review of youth support, echoed the sentiment that diagnosis has inappropriately become the key that unlocks help, creating pressure on individuals to seek a formal label.

The financial implications are significant. The Scottish Fiscal Commission projects the social‑security bill to reach £7.8 billion in 2027‑28, with ADP alone accounting for £4.2 billion. By 2030‑31 the total cost is forecast to rise to £9.2 billion, prompting scrutiny from auditors and opposition parties about long‑term sustainability. More than half of initial ADP applications are rejected, with an approval rate of 43 % and a denial rate of 54 %, figures that align closely with the system in England and Wales. Education Secretary Mairi McAllan defended the rigorous assessment process, emphasizing that claimants must demonstrate genuine need.

Scottish ministers argue that the generous approach reflects an investment in the population, even as they monitor proposals from England and Wales that could reshape youth support. First Minister John Swinney warned that changes south of the border might create "potentially some significant financial implications that could be negative" for Holyrood, especially if a £1 billion funding gap widens. Nonetheless, any savings realized through reforms in England could be offset by reallocating funds to other devolved services such as education or local employment programmes.

According to BBC News, the combination of a younger claimant profile, a higher share of mental‑health‑related applications, and rising costs places the Scottish welfare model at a crossroads. Policymakers must balance the desire to maintain a compassionate system with the fiscal realities of a tight budget settlement, while ensuring that support reaches those who need it without encouraging unnecessary medicalisation.

articles.title: Iraq Takes Control of Jurf al‑Sakhar Amid Militia Negotiations
articles.summary: Iraqi forces entered Jurf al‑Sakhar after a deal with Kataib Hezbollah, marking a step in Prime Minister Ali al‑Zaidi’s effort to curb militia power and corruption.
articles.content:
Iraqi government troops moved into Jurf al‑Sakhar, a town about 60 kilometres southwest of Baghdad, after a negotiated settlement with the Iran‑backed militia Kataib Hezbollah. The settlement ended a standoff that had threatened to erupt into armed conflict and allowed the state to re‑establish a presence in an area it had not accessed since the militia seized it from ISIL in 2014.

Under the agreement, a joint operations centre was set up in the town and a phased withdrawal of Kataib Hezbollah fighters was scheduled. The plan calls for the gradual replacement of militia units with an army brigade, a federal police brigade, an energy police regiment and two Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) brigades. The deployment is expected to take several weeks, with the aim of consolidating state authority while maintaining a security footprint.

The compromise was reportedly facilitated by direct Iranian involvement, with Esmail Qaani, head of the IRGC’s Quds Force, acting as a broker. Qaani, who previously fought alongside the PMF against ISIL, has long‑standing ties to several Iraqi militias, a factor that helped bring the two sides to the negotiating table.

Prime Minister Ali al‑Zaidi, who assumed office in May, has framed the operation as part of a broader anti‑corruption drive and an effort to bring weapons under federal control. He initially set a deadline for militias to submit their arms by the end of September, a date that was later extended to June 2027 after militias resisted the original timetable.

Baghdad’s security agenda also targets the use of Iraqi territory for attacks directed by Iran. Since the start of the US‑Israeli conflict with Iran, multiple Iraqi militias have pledged support for Tehran’s war effort, and the government has acknowledged that unauthorized strikes against neighboring states have been launched from within Iraq. The Jurf al‑Sakhar operation is therefore seen as a move to limit such capabilities.

"This area, which the state could not enter since 2014, did actually participate in Iran’s war effort, bombing Gulf countries, bombing US interests in Iraq," said Akeel Abbas, an expert on Iraqi affairs, speaking to Al Jazeera. He added that the town housed some of the most fortified militia positions and stored advanced weaponry.

Militias in Iraq operate under a complex legal framework. The PMF, created after a fatwa from senior Shia cleric Ali al‑Sistani, is officially recognised as part of the national security apparatus, granting its constituent groups semi‑official status. However, factions such as Kataib Hezbollah continue to function outside full state control, maintaining independent command structures and financing networks that critics say undermine governmental legitimacy.

"The remaining questions are how long this will take and what the armed groups will want in return," observed Zeidon Alkinani, founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, in an interview with Al Jazeera. He noted that the negotiated settlement, rather than a military clash, represented a positive development, though the ultimate outcome depends on subsequent phases of implementation.

Analysts caution that the security contingent sent by Baghdad includes militia‑aligned personnel, meaning the shift may amount to a change of uniforms rather than a true disarmament. Tallha Abdulrazaq, an Iraq security consultant, warned that without explicit steps to dismantle missile and drone production facilities linked to Iranian expertise, the arrangement could simply replace one set of Shia militias with another.

The town’s strategic significance is amplified by its history as the site of former President Saddam Hussein’s military‑industrial complex. By establishing a state presence there, Baghdad signals to the United States that it is removing a potential target for future strikes, a concern that resurfaced after US and Saudi retaliatory actions against PMF sites following attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure.

The Jurf al‑Sakhar deal illustrates the delicate balance the Iraqi government seeks between asserting sovereignty, curbing militia influence, and managing external pressures from Tehran and Washington. How the phased deployments unfold will determine whether the move translates into a lasting restoration of state authority or merely a reconfiguration of militia control.
